routes.title: Reaction time, road risk and injury

native.caption: Thinking distanceDistance travelled while the driver reacts.Braking distanceDistance travelled while braking to stop.The vehicle travels forward through the thinking interval, then through the braking interval. Total stopping distance includes both. This road illustration is not to scale.Original course illustration generated for Science 24; corrected for this review.

Attentive exampleApproximately one second in the illustration.Distracted exampleApproximately two to three seconds in the illustration. These are examples, not measured limits.Reaction times in this illustration are examples, not observed data or limits that permit driving. Fatigue, distraction and impairment can delay or disrupt a response.Original course illustration generated for Science 24.

videos.written: Written explanationA distance–time graph puts time on the horizontal axis and distance on the vertical. Its slope is distance change divided by time change. Velocity requires direction.

native.caption: Path distance800 m out + 800 m back = 1600 m.DisplacementStart and finish are at A, so displacement is 0 m.In this simplified 1600 m round trip, 800 m out and 800 m back return the traveller to the starting position. Distance is 1600 m; displacement is zero.Original course diagram authored for Science 24.

videos.written: Written explanationA flat position–time segment means no position change. A downward position line can mean motion in the negative direction, unlike an accumulated-distance graph.

routes.title: Travel time, reaction and stopping distance

videos.written: Written explanationBraking changes velocity over time. Reaction distance occurs first; road-tire grip and deceleration shape braking distance.
Written explanationMomentum p=mv. Use kilograms and metres per second for kg·m/s. Direction is part of velocity and therefore momentum.

native.caption: Shared velocityBoth model systems travel at +5 m/s.70 kg system70 kg × 5 m/s = +350 kg·m/s.750 kg system750 kg × 5 m/s = +3750 kg·m/s.Two simplified systems move at +5 m/s. Momentum is +350 kg·m/s for 70 kg and +3750 kg·m/s for 750 kg. The mass is what the model includes; momentum alone does not give collision force.Original course diagram authored for Science 24.

videos.written: Written explanationImpulse equals force times contact time and equals change in momentum. For the same Δp, a longer interaction reduces average force magnitude.

native.caption: Lower force, longer time100 N × 2 s = 200 N·s.Higher force, shorter time400 N × 0.5 s = 200 N·s.Read the graphEach rectangle has the same area. Force magnitudes are plotted; also state the direction.The existing 100 N × 2 s and 400 N × 0.5 s cases both give an impulse magnitude of 200 N·s. These simplified constant-force plots show magnitudes; the direction of impulse must also be stated.Original course diagram authored for Science 24.

Same momentum changeA 1000 kg vehicle goes from +10 m/s to rest: Δp = −10,000 kg·m/s.Shorter stop0.5 s gives a mean force of −20,000 N.Longer stop2.0 s gives a mean force of −5000 N.Read the graphAverage-force rectangles have equal area: impulse magnitude 10,000 N·s.For the same 1000 kg vehicle changing from +10 m/s to rest, Δp = −10,000 kg·m/s. A 0.5 s stop has mean force −20,000 N; a 2.0 s stop has mean force −5000 N. The plotted magnitudes have equal area.Original course diagram authored for Science 24.

routes.title: Collision systems and conservation of momentum

videos.written: Written explanationInternal interactions can change each object’s momentum while total system momentum remains constant when external impulse is negligible.
Written explanationAn occupant’s motion changes only when a force acts. Vehicle structure and restraints are designed to manage how that change occurs.

routes.title: Seat belts, child restraints and airbags

videos.written: Written explanationA belt positions and restrains the occupant; an airbag is supplemental. Vehicle and occupant outcomes depend on crash type, fit and design.

native.caption: Before a collisionThinking distance = speed × reaction time. Add braking distance to find total stopping distance.During an impactImpulse equals momentum change. For the same change, a longer time can reduce mean force.Reaction and braking determine stopping distance. During an impact, a longer stopping interval can reduce mean force for the same momentum change. Use the relevant model for each question.Original course diagram authored for Science 24.
